lessons.title: What happens in second phase
lessons.html:
After inspection

In first phase evisceration the bird was opened and the guts were pulled out to hang beside the carcass for inspection. Once the meat inspector has passed the bird, second phase evisceration begins. In this phase the organs are separated, the useful parts (giblets) are saved, and the bird is cleaned inside and out so it is ready for chilling.

Main steps in second phase

  1. Giblet harvesting – the heart, liver and gizzard are removed from the viscera pack.
  2. Removing the intestines – the rest of the guts are dropped into the offal channel.
  3. Cropping – removing the crop, gullet and windpipe from the neck.
  4. Lung removal – the lungs sit against the backbone and are removed with a vacuum tube or by hand.
  5. Neck removal – the neck is cut off; it may be packed as a giblet.
  6. Final check – looking for leftover organs, feathers, faeces and bruises.
  7. Inside-outside washing – sprays wash the inside and outside of the bird.

After this the bird goes to the chiller.

Only passed birds

Never take giblets from a bird that the inspector has condemned or held. Organs from a sick bird must not enter the food chain. If you are not sure whether a bird has been passed, ask before you work on it.

Why it matters

Leftover lungs, crop or windpipe make the carcass look bad and can hold germs. Faeces or bile on the meat spread germs and spoil the taste. A good second phase gives a clean carcass that keeps longer and sells for a better price. It also saves the giblets, which the plant sells as livers, gizzards, hearts and necks.

Like first phase, this work is done in the clean area of the plant. The Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 requires that meat is handled hygienically from here to despatch.

lessons.title: Harvesting and cleaning giblets
lessons.html:
Saving the edible organs

Giblets are the edible organs: heart, liver, gizzard and often the neck. Many South African customers buy livers and gizzards, so the plant wants them clean and whole.

Liver

  • Separate the liver from the guts carefully.
  • Remove the gall bladder (the small green sac) without breaking it. Green bile stains the liver and makes it bitter.
  • Throw away livers with spots, a bad colour or bile stains, as your plant says.

Heart

  • Pull or cut the heart from the viscera.
  • Remove the heart sac and large blood vessels if the spec says so.

Gizzard

  1. Cut the gizzard from the gut.
  2. Split it open (by machine or knife) and wash out the grit and food.
  3. Peel off the tough yellow lining. Gizzard peeler machines have rollers that pull the lining off.
  4. Check that no lining or grit is left.

Giblet hygiene

  • Put giblets into clean trays or flumes (water channels), not on the floor.
  • Chill them quickly; giblets spoil faster than meat.
  • Keep livers, hearts and gizzards apart if the plant packs them separately.

Safety

Gizzard peelers have rollers that can pull in fingers and gloves.

  • Never push a gizzard into the rollers with your fingers.
  • Stop and lock out the machine before clearing or cleaning it.
  • Keep guards in place.
  • Use a sharp knife and a cut-resistant glove.

lessons.title: Final cleaning and quality checks
lessons.html:
Making sure the carcass is clean

Lung removal and cropping

Lungs are pressed against the ribs and backbone. In most plants a vacuum gun sucks them out. Put the nozzle in carefully so that you do not break ribs or tear the skin. The crop is pulled out by a cropping machine or by hand through the neck opening.

Final check

At the final check station look inside and outside each bird. Look for:

  • pieces of lung, crop, windpipe or gut left inside;
  • faeces or bile on the meat;
  • feathers and pin feathers;
  • bruises, broken bones and torn skin.

Remove what you can by hand. Send birds that need trimming to the rework or trim station. Faecal contamination must be dealt with exactly as your plant's food safety plan says.

Inside-outside washer

Check that all spray nozzles are working. A blocked nozzle means birds leave dirty. Report it at once. Washing helps, but it does not make a contaminated bird safe – careful work in evisceration is the best protection.

Records

Your supervisor may ask you to count faults, for example lungs left in 50 birds. Write the counts clearly on the sheet with the time and your name.

End of shift

  • Stop and lock out the machines.
  • Clean knives, trays, machines and floors with the right chemicals, wearing the gloves and eye protection on the label.
  • Rinse well so no chemicals are left on surfaces that touch meat.

Key points

  • Second phase starts only after the inspector has passed the bird.
  • Harvest heart, liver and gizzard; remove the gall bladder without breaking it.
  • Remove lungs, crop and windpipe, then check and wash each bird.
  • Never push gizzards into peeler rollers with your fingers.
  • Chill giblets quickly and keep them off the floor.
